title: Jethro's advice (Exodus 18)
hook: Moses' father-in-law tells him he can't judge everyone alone

segments.voice: Yesterday, manna: bread from heaven, gathered one morning at a time. Your line was enough for today. Did you stop at enough, even once? Day ninety-three.

At some workplaces there's one person who answers every question, signs off on every decision, stays late every night, and is quietly falling apart. The parent who does all of it because it's faster than explaining. In the wilderness, Moses is that person. From morning until evening, a line of people stands in front of him, waiting for him to settle their arguments. And then his father-in-law comes to visit, watches for one day, and says something very plain. Today: Jethro's advice.
screen: `THE ONE WHO DOES IT ALL.` → `A LINE FROM MORNING TO EVENING.` → `THE FATHER-IN-LAW WATCHES.`

segments.voice: Jethro, Yitro in Hebrew, is a priest of Midian, not an Israelite. Moses married his daughter Zipporah years before, when he ran away from Egypt. Now Jethro hears everything God did for the people, and he comes out to the desert, brings Moses's wife and sons, and rejoices with him. The next morning he sits and watches Moses work. And he asks a very plain question: why are you sitting alone, with everyone standing around you from morning to evening? Moses says, they come to me to ask of God, and I judge between them. And Jethro answers, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "The thing that thou doest is not good." You'll wear yourself out, you and the people with you, "for the thing is too heavy for thee; thou art not able to perform it thyself alone." Then he gives him a plan. Teach everyone the laws, so they know the way. Find capable people who fear God, who love truth, who hate a bribe. Put them in charge of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. Let them handle the small cases, and bring you only the hard ones. And Moses, the man who spoke with God at the burning bush, listens to his father-in-law and does all of it. And here's a detail the tradition keeps: the Torah portion that holds the Ten Commandments is named Yitro, after an outsider. Good advice, it suggests, can come from outside the camp. And a whole system of judges began with someone saying, gently, you can't do this alone.
screen: `A PRIEST OF MIDIAN COMES TO VISIT.` · `THE THING IS TOO HEAVY FOR THEE.` · `THOUSANDS, HUNDREDS, FIFTIES, TENS.` · `A PORTION NAMED FOR AN OUTSIDER.` · then, large: `THOU ART NOT ABLE TO PERFORM IT ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hand one task to someone else. Settle, and breathe. Picture the line of things waiting for you this week, the way Moses saw a line of people. Walk down it slowly. Find one thing someone else could do, maybe not your way, maybe not as fast, but well enough. A colleague, a partner, a child, a friend, a service. Choose it. Picture yourself asking, and picture them saying yes. Then notice what your shoulders feel like when it's off them. The bell holds the time.
Jethro's advice. A father-in-law from Midian tells Moses the work is too heavy for one person, and helps him share it.
Your line: you can't carry it alone. Today, ask for help with one thing, out loud, before it gets too heavy. Day ninety-three.

howItsDone: Parashat Yitro, which includes Jethro's visit and the Ten Commandments, is read in synagogue each winter as part of the yearly Torah cycle.

a whole Torah portion is named after Jethro
Parashat Yitro, and it contains the Ten Commandments.
he listened to his father-in-law and did everything he said.

fork.setup: you're Moses. you've led the people out of Egypt. your father-in-law says you're doing it all wrong. what do you do?
options: thank him and change how you work.
explain that God chose you, not him.
fork.reveal: Moses listens and does all that Jethro says. the man of the burning bush takes advice from an outsider.

original.note: Hebrew: Jethro. a midrash, quoted by Rashi, links the name to yeter, more.

trapdoor: what you thought: a family visit.
what it means: a father-in-law tells Moses the work is too heavy for one, and helps him set up a shared system of judges.
what a scholar hears: the portion bearing an outsider's name comes just before Sinai; commentators debate whether Jethro's visit happened before or after the giving of the Torah.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 18:17 and 18:18.
Qualities of the leaders (18:21) paraphrased: able men, fearing God, men of truth, hating unjust gain.
Original note: link of Yitro to yeter (more/abundance) is from midrash (e.g. Rashi on 18:1, citing an added portion to the Torah). Confirm or simplify.
Timing debate (before or after Sinai) is in Zevachim 116a and Rashi/Ibn Ezra; confirm citation.
Parashat Yitro is read in winter (Shevat) in most years. Confirm.

Editor review: the teach said Parashat Yitro comes 'right before' the Ten Commandments; it contains them (Exodus 18–20), as the myth item already said; fixed. Hook no longer tells the listener 'maybe you are someone like this' and drops the invented 'what nobody else has dared to say' and 'every single one'; cut the superlatives 'the first system of courts' and 'the greatest prophet'; the name note now credits the midrash.
